excerpt: Original Medicare splits hospital, doctor, and drug coverage into separate parts, but Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare plus Part D can bring them together.
author: David Haass
imageAlt: What Medicare options cover hospital, doctor, and prescriptions together?
keyTakeaways: Original Medicare (Parts A and B) covers hospital and doctor visits but never includes prescription drug coverage
Part D drug coverage must always be purchased separately, whether through a standalone plan or bundled into Medicare Advantage
Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans, often called MA-PD plans, typically combine hospital, medical, and drug coverage into one plan with a network
Pairing Original Medicare with a Medigap policy and a standalone Part D plan offers more provider flexibility but requires managing three separate pieces
Before enrolling in Medicare Advantage, confirm your doctors, specialists, and hospital are in the plan's network
seoTitle: Medicare Plans That Cover It All: What You Need to Know
seoDescription: Learn how Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare plus Part D can combine hospital, doctor, and prescription drug coverage into one simple planT.

sections.content: A single Medicare card does not automatically bundle your hospital stays, doctor visits, and prescription drugs into one neat package. That surprises a lot of people. Original Medicare actually splits coverage into separate parts, and prescriptions almost always require a decision you make on your own.

The good news is that two clear paths exist for pulling hospital care, medical visits, and drug coverage together. Understanding how each path works, and what it costs, makes the rest of your Medicare decisions much easier.

sections.text: The Building Blocks of Medicare Coverage

sections.content: Medicare breaks coverage into four distinct parts, and each one handles a different piece of your care. [Part A covers inpatient](/faqs/does-medicare-cover-hospice/) hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care, and hospice. Part B covers outpatient services like doctor visits, lab work, and preventive screenings.

Part D is the piece that trips people up most often. It covers prescription drugs, but it is sold separately and is never automatically included with Original Medicare. Part C, known as [Medicare Advantage](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-advantage-vs-original-medicare/), is where many of these pieces get combined into a single plan.

sections.calloutText: Original Medicare (Parts A and B) comes from the federal government and does not include drug coverage. Medicare Advantage (Part C) is sold by private insurers and often bundles hospital, medical, and drug coverage into one plan. See our [Medicare Advantage vs. Original Medicare comparison](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-advantage-vs-original-medicare/) for a full breakdown.

sections.text: Option 1: Medicare Advantage Plans With Drug Coverage

sections.content: [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/)s, often called MA-PD plans when they include drug coverage, are the closest thing Medicare offers to a true all-in-one option. A single plan typically covers your hospital stays, doctor visits, and prescriptions under one card and one insurer. Most plans also add extras like dental, vision, or hearing benefits that Original Medicare does not cover.

The tradeoff is that these plans usually work through a network, similar to an HMO or PPO structure you might recognize from employer coverage. Your preferred doctor or specialist needs to be in that network, or your costs can rise sharply. Referrals may also be required for specialist visits, depending on the plan type.

sections.calloutTitle: Check Your Doctors Before You Enroll
sections.calloutText: Before choosing a [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/), confirm that your current doctors, specialists, and preferred hospital are in the plan's network. A plan with a low premium is not a good deal if it forces you to switch providers. The [Medicare Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov) lets you compare plans available in your area, including their networks, costs, and covered drugs, side by side.

sections.text: Option 2: Original Medicare Plus a Part D Plan

sections.content: The second path keeps Original Medicare's Part A and Part B as your foundation, then adds a standalone Part D plan for prescriptions. This combination gives you broader provider flexibility since Original Medicare is accepted by nearly any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare nationwide. You are not locked into a network tied to a single insurance company.

Many people pair this combination with a [[Medicare Supplement](/faqs/medicare-supplement-vs-medicare-advantage/) (Medigap) policy](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-supplement-plans/), which helps cover the out-of-pocket costs Original Medicare leaves behind, such as coinsurance and hospital deductibles. Common standardized options include Plan G and Plan N, each offering a different balance of premium cost and out-of-pocket coverage. A Medigap plan does not include drug coverage, so the Part D plan still needs to be purchased separately. Together, these three pieces (Part A, Part B, a Medigap plan, and Part D) create a different kind of all-in-one coverage, just not from a single policy.

sections.title: Comparing the Two Main Coverage Paths
rows: Bundled into one plan, typically with a $0 to moderate monthly premium on top of the standard Part B premium
Purchased as separate pieces: Part B premium, plus a Part D premium that varies by plan, plus any Medigap premium
Often restricted to an HMO or PPO network; out-of-network care may cost more or not be covered
Accepted nationwide by any provider who takes Medicare, with no network restrictions
Frequently included as part of the plan at no extra premium
Not included, purchased separately through standalone dental, vision, or hearing plans
Up to $9,250 for in-network services, per CMS.gov
No cap on Part A and Part B cost-sharing unless paired with a Medigap plan, which can bring out-of-pocket costs close to $0 for covered services
Often required for HMO plans; some PPO plans do not require referrals
Not required; you can see any specialist who accepts Medicare
sections.footnote: Maximum out-of-pocket figures reflect 2026 Medicare Advantage limits and can vary by plan. Source: CMS.gov.

sections.content: Cost is usually the deciding factor once coverage and network questions are settled. Original Medicare has set premiums and deductibles that apply nationwide, while Medicare Advantage and Part D premiums vary by plan and location.

sections.title: 2026 Medicare Cost Snapshot
rows: Part A daily coinsurance (days 61-90 of hospital stay)
Part A skilled nursing facility coinsurance (days 21-100)
sections.footnote: Figures according to CMS.gov and Medicare.gov. Higher-income beneficiaries may pay IRMAA surcharges on top of standard Part B and Part D premiums. Please confirm current amounts on [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov) before making coverage decisions.

sections.calloutText: IRMAA is not a single cutoff but a series of income brackets, each tied to a different surcharge amount on top of standard Part B and Part D premiums. Your 2026 IRMAA tier is based on your reported income from two years earlier, and the surcharge increases step by step as income rises through each bracket, according to CMS.gov. These surcharges apply regardless of whether you choose Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare with a separate Part D plan. If your income has dropped due to a life-changing event such as retirement, divorce, or the death of a spouse, you can request a reconsideration by filing SSA Form SSA-44 with the Social Security Administration. Current IRMAA brackets and thresholds are published each year on [Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov).

sections.content: I always tell people to run the math on total yearly cost, not just the monthly premium. A [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) with a $0 premium can still cost more over a year than a Medigap and Part D combination if you need several specialist visits or a hospital stay. Consider a 66-year-old taking two generic prescriptions and seeing one specialist twice a year. A $0 premium Medicare Advantage plan might charge a specialist copay each visit plus drug copays at the pharmacy, while a Medigap plan with a monthly premium paired with a low-cost Part D plan could cover most of those same visits and medications with little left to pay out of pocket. Running both scenarios side by side, using your actual visits and prescriptions from the past year, is the only reliable way to see which path costs less for you. The Medicare Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov is a good starting point for comparing actual plan costs and coverage in your area.

sections.text: Common Mistakes People Make When Combining Coverage

sections.content: Several patterns show up again and again when people piece together their hospital, medical, and drug coverage. Catching these early can save real money and frustration down the road.

items: **Skipping Part D entirely** because you do not take medications now, then facing a late enrollment penalty later, which you can estimate with our [Part D penalty calculator](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-part-d-penalty-calculator/)

**Assuming Medigap includes drug coverage**, when in fact every Medigap plan, including Plan G and Plan N, excludes prescriptions, as explained in our [Medigap guide](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-supplement-plans/)
**Choosing a [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/) based on premium alone** without checking if your doctors are in-network
**Missing the Medigap guaranteed issue window**, which can lead to medical underwriting and higher premiums later
**Forgetting to compare plan formularies**, since two Part D plans can cover the same drug at very different costs
**Overlooking Extra Help (the Low-Income Subsidy, or LIS)**, a program that can lower Part D premiums and copays for those who qualify based on income and resources
**Assuming you have missed your chance to enroll**, when a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) may apply if you have had a qualifying life event such as losing other coverage or moving

sections.calloutTitle: The Part D Late Enrollment Penalty
sections.calloutText: If you go 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage after becoming eligible, Medicare adds a penalty to your Part D premium for as long as you have coverage. The penalty is calculated using the national base premium, which was $38.99 in a recent year, multiplied by the number of full months you went without coverage, according to Medicare.gov. You can estimate your own potential penalty using our [Part D penalty calculator](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-part-d-penalty-calculator/).

sections.text: How to Decide Which Path Fits Your Situation

sections.content: There is no single right answer here, since the best combination depends on your doctors, your budget, and how often you expect to need care. Someone managing a chronic condition with frequent specialist visits may value the predictable costs a [Medigap plan](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-supplement-plans/), such as Plan G or Plan N, offers. Someone who travels often or wants extra benefits like dental coverage may lean toward [Medicare Advantage](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-advantage-vs-original-medicare/).

items: **List your current doctors and medications**, then check which plans in your area include them

**Compare total estimated yearly costs**, not just monthly premiums, across both coverage paths, using the [Medicare Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov) to see actual plan options and pricing where you live
**Decide how much flexibility you need** in choosing providers outside a plan network

**Check your enrollment window** to avoid penalties or medical underwriting delays, using our [AEP and enrollment period explainer](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-enrollment-periods/), and find out whether a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) applies to your situation
**Talk with a licensed Medicare agent** who can walk through plan options available where you live

sections.calloutTitle: You Have More Time Than You Think
sections.calloutText: Most people are not locked into one choice forever. [Medicare Advantage plan](/faqs/medicare-advantage-open-enrollment-period/)s can be reviewed and changed during the Annual Enrollment Period each fall, giving you a built-in opportunity to adjust your coverage as your needs change. Special Enrollment Periods (SEP) may also be available outside of that window if you have a qualifying life event. Learn more in our [AEP and enrollment period explainer](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-enrollment-periods/).

faqs.question: Does Original Medicare automatically include prescription drug coverage?
faqs.answer: No. Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) does not include prescription drug coverage. You need to enroll in a separate Part D plan or choose a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug benefits.

faqs.question: Can I get hospital, doctor, and drug coverage from one single plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, through a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage, often labeled MA-PD. These plans bundle Part A, Part B, and Part D benefits into one policy sold by a private insurer. See our [Medicare Advantage vs. Original Medicare comparison](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-advantage-vs-original-medicare/) for more detail.

faqs.question: Is it better to choose Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare with Medigap and Part D?
faqs.answer: It depends on your priorities. Medicare Advantage often costs less upfront but limits you to a network, while Original Medicare with a Medigap plan, such as Plan G or Plan N, and Part D costs more monthly but offers nationwide provider access and predictable out-of-pocket costs. Our [Medigap guide](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-supplement-plans/) can help you compare further.

faqs.question: What happens if I wait too long to enroll in Part D?
faqs.answer: You may face a late enrollment penalty added to your monthly Part D premium for as long as you have coverage. This penalty is based on the national base premium, which was $38.99 in a recent year, and increases the longer you go without creditable drug coverage, according to Medicare.gov. If you have limited income and resources, the Extra Help (Low-Income Subsidy) program may reduce or eliminate this burden. Use our [Part D penalty calculator](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-part-d-penalty-calculator/) to estimate your own penalty.

faqs.question: Will my doctors be covered no matter which option I choose?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Original Medicare is accepted by most providers nationwide, but Medicare Advantage plans often restrict you to an in-network list. Always confirm your specific doctors and hospitals before enrolling in any plan.

faqs.question: Can I switch between these coverage options later if my needs change?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Annual Enrollment Period each fall lets you switch Medicare Advantage plans or move between Medicare Advantage and Original Medicare. A Special Enrollment Period (SEP) may also let you make changes outside this window if you have a qualifying life event, such as moving or losing other coverage. Switching into a Medigap plan later may require medical underwriting unless you qualify for a guaranteed issue right. See our [AEP and enrollment period explainer](https://www.medicarefaq.com/medicare-enrollment-periods/) for key dates.

faqs.question: I am worried about making the wrong choice. How can I compare options without pressure?
faqs.answer: A licensed Medicare agent can walk through your doctors, medications, and budget to compare plans available in your area, with no obligation to enroll on the spot. You can also use the [Medicare Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov) on your own to compare plans side by side. This gives you a clear comparison before you commit to anything.

faqs.question: What can I do if an IRMAA surcharge no longer reflects my current income?
faqs.answer: If you have had a life-changing event such as retirement, reduced work hours, divorce, or the death of a spouse, you can file SSA Form SSA-44 with the Social Security Administration to request a reconsideration of your IRMAA surcharge based on your more recent income.

sections.content: Combining hospital, medical, and drug coverage does not have to mean sorting through dozens of pages of plan documents on your own. A side-by-side comparison, built around your actual doctors, medications, and budget, turns a confusing decision into a manageable one. The [Medicare Plan Finder tool on Medicare.gov](https://www.medicare.gov) is a free resource that lets you compare Medicare Advantage and Part D plans available in your area.

If you want a clearer picture of what is available where you live, a licensed Medicare agent can walk through your options and explain the tradeoffs in plain language. There is no cost to compare plans, and you decide the pace.
